opus-5.5.text:
I think it takes much more time and accumulation than people expect, and the accumulation is of a different kind than for a chat model.

With a chat model, much of the capability comes from pretraining. You scale the data and compute, do reasonable post-training, and you get a model that answers questions well. An agentic model has to do something much harder: act over many steps in an environment, use tools, read feedback, recover from mistakes, and pursue a goal over a long horizon. That ability doesn't come for free from next-token prediction on internet text, because the internet contains very little data about the *process* of solving a long task. It mostly contains the results.

So the accumulation happens on several levels at once.

The first is infrastructure. To train agentic behavior you need large-scale reinforcement learning, which means thousands of environments running in parallel, sandboxes, tool execution, long rollouts, and stable training at scale. Building that infrastructure takes a long time, and much of the work is unglamorous engineering. If the infra isn't solid, nothing upstream matters.

The second is environments and tasks. You need a large variety of realistic tasks with verifiable outcomes, so the model gets a meaningful reward signal. In some sense this is the new "data." Before, we accumulated tokens; now we accumulate environments. Their diversity and quality determine how well the model generalizes.

The third is the base model. The base model's capability is the ceiling for RL. With a weak base model, RL mostly amplifies its weaknesses. That's why we still care a lot about pretraining efficiency, things like optimizers and architecture choices that give you more intelligence per unit of compute. A good base model makes agentic training far more efficient.

The fourth, which people often underestimate, is the team's understanding: knowing which reward signals are hackable, how to keep long-horizon training stable, how to balance generality against specific skills like coding or search. That knowledge comes only from running many experiments and failing many times. You can't shortcut it by reading papers.

So I don't think it's something you can catch up on in a few months by throwing compute at it. It's more like compound interest: each layer of accumulation makes the next iteration faster. Teams that started thinking seriously about agents early, and invested in the infra and environments, will have a real advantage. But it's also still early. The paradigm is moving fast, and there's plenty of room for whoever has the clearest technical judgment and executes most consistently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large-scale reinforcement learning as part of the required infrastructure, but does not present more end-to-end RL as a later stage after an initial resource-accumulation phase.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there's no shortcut, but the accumulation isn't the kind people usually imagine. People tend to think you need a huge dataset or some secret architecture. What you actually need is a long sequence of correct decisions about what to scale, and you only earn those decisions by running into the wrong ones first.

For us, the first layer of accumulation was pretraining. You have to have a base model that already has a strong world model, strong coding ability, strong long-context ability, because an agent is basically a model that has to act over many steps without losing the thread. If the foundation is weak, no amount of agent scaffolding fixes it. That took us years, and a lot of it looked like boring infrastructure work: data pipelines, training stability, figuring out how to make the model learn efficiently per token.

The second layer is reinforcement learning on top of that, and this is where I think the real time cost is. Agentic behavior is not something you can annotate your way into. You have to build environments where the model can try, fail, and get a signal. Building those environments, and building the RL systems that can run them at scale with long rollouts, is a different engineering discipline from pretraining. We underestimated how much of the problem would become a systems problem rather than an algorithm problem.

And then there's a third layer that's harder to quantify, which is taste. Knowing which benchmarks are real signals and which are just noise, knowing when a capability is truly generalizing versus when the model has learned to game your evaluation. That kind of judgment compounds across the team over time, and it's honestly what separates groups that keep improving from groups that plateau.

So when people ask how long it takes, I'd say the visible part, the training run, is the shortest part. The accumulation is in the years before it, and most of that accumulation is learning what not to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate presents reinforcement learning as a second layer after pretraining, with environments and long rollouts. It does not clearly describe this as more end-to-end RL following an initial phase of resource accumulation.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two kinds of accumulation. One is improving the underlying model—its reasoning, its ability to use tools, and its ability to recover when something goes wrong. The other is learning from actual tasks: what users want to delegate, where the agent fails, and how to evaluate whether it really completed the work.

Those two processes have to develop together. If you only improve the model on isolated benchmarks, you may miss the problems that appear when it has to take many steps. But if you only build the application, you eventually run into the limits of the model.

So I wouldn’t think of it simply as needing a certain number of months or years. The important thing is whether you have a productive feedback loop: deploy something, observe failures, turn those failures into useful training and evaluation, and improve the next version. That accumulation takes time, but the quality of the loop matters as much as the time itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes model improvement and task-based learning as concurrent feedback processes, but does not identify more end-to-end reinforcement learning as a later development stage following initial resource accumulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different timelines. One is the time it takes to build a model that can demonstrate agentic behavior. The other is the time it takes to make that behavior reliable enough to be useful. You can get an impressive demonstration fairly quickly, but reliability requires much more accumulation.

For an agent, the model has to make a sequence of decisions, use tools, observe the results, and recover when something goes wrong. Even if each individual step is usually correct, errors compound over a long task. So improving the underlying model is only part of the work. You also need good training environments, feedback, and evaluations that tell you whether the agent actually completed the task.

The accumulation that matters is the ability to keep running that cycle: identify failures, understand what caused them, improve the training, and measure whether the improvement generalizes. That takes time, but it isn’t simply a matter of waiting or having started earlier. A better approach can change the speed of progress substantially. I would look at how quickly a team learns from each iteration, rather than just how many months it has spent building an agent.

r001.rationale: The response discusses accumulating training environments, feedback, and iterative learning, but it does not identify an initial resource-accumulation phase followed by a later stage of more end-to-end reinforcement learning.
